title: The Lesson Observation Model is Broken
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Emanuele makes a direct case that high-stakes, short-window lesson observation is an antiquated practice that cannot capture what good teaching looks like. His premise is that effective teaching is a responsive toolbox rather than a silver bullet, and that its real texture is messy and slow: five quiet minutes diagnosing a misconception with mini-whiteboards, ten methodical minutes modelling a process, a supervised practice phase where students are deliberately not talking. An observer arriving for ten to twenty minutes expects a highlight reel and will see diligence rather than fireworks. The problem compounds when a pre-written checklist supplies the boxes — buzzing engagement, flawless explicit teaching, perfect books, visible checking on Pupil Premium and SEN students — because anything not performed in the window goes unticked, and the feedback then tells the teacher to 'do more of X' as though they never do it. His controlling image is the Louvre: judging the plain yellow top-right corner of the Mona Lisa and concluding it is not a masterpiece. The fix he proposes is threefold — open by asking the teacher to narrate when the great moment happened, agree the focus and timing of the visit in advance, and empower observers to take a professional rain check when they arrive during quiet practice. The argument ends by recasting observation as peer coaching rather than performance review.
points: The structural critique is a sampling problem: a twelve-minute slice cannot evidence a sixty-minute sequence, so the instrument mismeasures precisely the practices schools say they want.
The checklist converts absence-of-observation into absence-of-practice, which is how well-intentioned feedback ends up implying a teacher never does what they in fact do regularly.
Emanuele's first fix inverts the authority of the visit — the observer opens by asking the teacher to identify and describe the lesson's real learning moment, corroborated by student work.
Pre-agreeing the exact moment an observer walks in is proposed as normal professional communication rather than as gaming the observation.

The 'professional rain check' is the most immediately adoptable idea: an observer who arrives during a low-stakes quiz or silent practice should be free to return later rather than judge what is in front of them.
quotes: As a teacher with over a decade in the secondary classroom, and having spent countless hours immersed in the best available research, I’ve learned one crucial truth: there is no single “silver bullet” in teaching. Our practice is a complex, responsive toolbox of strategies.
We need to be honest: the current observation model is broken. It’s an antiquated practice that fails to capture what great teaching truly looks like, and here are the reasons why.
The core flaw lies in the time limit. A colleague, often a well-meaning observer, walks in for 10 to 20 minutes and expects to witness a condensed highlight reel of “amazing teaching moments.

If those specific, performative moments don’t occur within the 20-minute window, the box remains unticked. The resulting feedback often instructs the teacher to “do more of X,” which implies they aren’t doing it at all.

The observed teacher knows the truth: those moments happen. They happen before the observer arrived, or they’ll happen five minutes after they leave, or maybe the next lesson (not everything must happen in every single lesson). The result is a toxic experience a good teacher is left feeling they’ve failed because a 60-minute process was judged by a 12-minute slice.

This is the equivalent of walking into the Louvre, looking at only the top-right corner of the Mona Lisa, a plain, empty yellow space, and concluding that it is not a masterpiece. The truth is, you simply missed the masterpiece.

So, how do we fix this? The answer is simple, polite, and respectful of the teacher’s expertise. We need to shift the focus from a judgmental snapshot to a professional conversation about the entire learning journey.
